Header:
Date: 2025-05-14
Time: 15:00 - 16:02 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE); Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE); Tom Nguyen (Redwood Security Engineer); Priya Menon (Nova CISO); Carlos Vega (Nova Cloud Architect); Marta Gomez (Nova Infra)
Links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/security, https://redwood.ai/docs/private-vpc, example SOC2: /redwood/soc2-2024.pdf

Optional auto-generated Summary: Medium confidence - speaker labels sometimes generic.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me are Lena and Tom. How are you all?
[00:06] Priya: Hi Samir, thanks. I'm Priya, CISO at Nova. Carlos and Marta are with me. We've got about an hour, thanks for taking the time.
[00:10] Samir: Great, want to confirm agenda: SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO, audit logs and SIEM, encryption/KMS options, then deep-dive on private VPC network design — ingress/egress and firewalling. Sound good?
[00:18] Carlos: Yep that's right, especially want clarity on egress controls and how we can restrict traffic.
[00:22] Lena: Perfect. I'll start with a quick overview of our private deployment modes and then Tom will take the security specifics.
[00:28] Lena: So, Redwood Private can be deployed with a private control plane in your VPC or via our hosted control plane with VPC peering/PrivateLink; for fully air-gapped on-prem we offer an on-prem package. We support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations.
[00:38] Marta: Can you clarify the difference between private control plane and hosted control plane again?
[00:41] Lena: Sure — private control plane means the control plane components run in your account/VPC, you control networking and KMS. Hosted control plane means Redwood manages the control plane but we provide a system-to-system PrivateLink endpoint so control traffic doesn't traverse the public internet. There are tradeoffs: private control plane gives max isolation, hosted control plane is faster to set up.
[00:54] Priya: For our compliance posture we prefer private control plane — we need keys never leaving our KMS and audit logs under our retention.
[00:58] Tom: Totally understood. On KMS we support AWS KMS customer-managed keys; we also have integrations for HSM-backed keys for FIPS-level requirements. Keys can be configured so that only a small subset of service principals can decrypt.
[01:06] Carlos: How does key rotation work? Do you support automatic rotation, and do you retain old keys to decrypt historical logs?
[01:11] Tom: We support automatic rotation with a configurable policy, and we maintain a key wrapping scheme so previously encrypted artifacts remain decryptable as long as the old keys exist in your KMS. For stricter controls you can opt to rotate manually and manage retention.
[01:20] Priya: Audit logs — we need full request/response metadata and the ability to forward logs to our Splunk instance. Retention 7 years. Thoughts?
[01:26] Lena: We emit audit logs for control plane and data plane events. For private control plane, logs are stored in your account and you can configure forwarding to your SIEM via S3 or direct ingestion endpoints. Retention policy you can enforce via lifecycle rules. For hosted we can stream logs via a customer-owned Kinesis or S3.
[01:38] Marta: Are request/response bodies included? We cannot send PII to third parties.
[01:42] Tom: By default, we redact sensitive payloads from control plane logs. For data plane (model inputs/outputs), in private deployments you control whether those are stored; we can disable retention and avoid persisting response bodies. We'll need to agree on the pilot's data handling config.
[01:54] Carlos: Network — we need to ensure no unwanted egress. Can Redwood function without NAT to the internet, or do you require outbound connectivity?
[01:59] Lena: In private control plane mode inside your VPC, you can have no public NAT. However, some components — like pulling container images or OS patching — may need egress or a private mirror. For runtime inference, if everything is in your VPC and model artifacts are pre-provisioned, we can operate with strict egress rules, and communication is within the VPC/subnet.
[02:12] Samir: A common pattern is to use an outbound proxy or VPC endpoint for controlled egress, and use PrivateLink for control-plane API calls.
[02:18] Priya: Firewalling — do you have a recommended set of ports and CIDR ranges to allow?
[02:21] Lena: Yes, we'll provide a baseline architecture diagram and firewall policy. Typically you need intra-cluster ports (gRPC and HTTP) and restricted control-plane endpoints via PrivateLink; for pod-to-pod traffic we recommend security groups limiting to the cluster CIDR. We'll send a proposed list.
[02:34] Carlos: How about ingress? We need to ensure only our load balancer can reach the model endpoints.
[02:38] Tom: For ingress we recommend placing model endpoints behind an internal ALB/NLB with mTLS to ensure mutual authentication. We support configuring TLS termination either at the customer LB or within the cluster; mTLS provides the extra layer.
[02:48] Marta: Do you support AWS PrivateLink or Transit Gateway? We prefer PrivateLink for control plane connectivity.
[02:52] Lena: Yes, PrivateLink is supported and is our recommended approach for hosted-control-plane customers who want minimal internet exposure. Transit Gateway is also supported for enterprise network topologies.
[02:59] Priya: SSO and RBAC — deep dive. We require SAML with SCIM provisioning and strict RBAC.
[03:03] Samir: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with least privilege by default; you can create custom roles and map to groups from your IdP.
[03:12] Tom: Additionally, all admin actions are logged and we provide an audit trail with user id, timestamp, action, and resource. These can be exported to your SIEM.
[03:19] Priya: Can you guarantee that only a subset of Redwood engineers have access for support? We need time-bound Just-in-Time access and auditability.
[03:25] Lena: For private control plane, you can completely avoid giving Redwood console access. For hosted control plane, we offer a time-bound support access flow with JIT and we require customer approval; all sessions are recorded and audited.
[03:36] Carlos: Latency concern — if we run in a cross-account VPC with PrivateLink to Redwood, is there any notable latency penalty?
[03:40] Samir: Latency is minimal for control plane calls. For model inference if everything is in your VPC, there is negligible extra latency. We'll include performance numbers in the follow-up doc.
[03:47] Marta: About image provisioning and OS patches you mentioned earlier — can we pre-build images and keep them in our ECR to avoid internet pulls?
[03:52] Lena: Absolutely, you can host images in ECR; the runtime can pull from your ECR via IAM roles. That eliminates public internet pulls.
[03:58] Priya: Regarding encryption at rest for model artifacts and KV cache, is that using our KMS keys?
[04:02] Tom: Yes, for private deployments model artifacts and KV cache can be encrypted with your KMS CMKs. We also support envelope encryption where the service uses a data key wrapped by your KMS.
[04:10] Carlos: For regulatory reasons we need to guarantee data residency in a single region and forbid cross-region replication. Can you ensure that?
[04:16] Lena: Yes, in private deployments we can pin everything to your region and we do not replicate across regions unless explicitly configured. We'll document the defaults and controls.
[04:24] Samir: Let's talk about network design specifics — I'll hand off to Lena for a quick example architecture and then Tom will cover firewall rules.
[04:29] Lena: Example: Customer VPC with private subnets hosting Redwood runtime. ECR for images, S3 for logs/artifacts (optional in customer account), PrivateLink endpoint to hosted control plane OR private control plane in the same account. Ingress via internal NLB with security groups allowing LB CIDR only. Egress via NAT or egress VPC endpoint to your proxy.
[04:45] Carlos: For NLB, do you recommend internal or external? Internal.
[04:48] Lena: Yes internal NLB recommended. Also recommend security groups that are locked to the LB's ENIs and K8s worker security groups.
[04:55] Tom: Firewall rules: deny by default. Allow only required ports: 443 for control plane (TLS), gRPC ports for intra-service comms (we'll provide exact ports), and management ports only from the jump host or bastion. Disable SSH on nodes and use session manager where possible.
[05:10] Priya: What about egress to telemetry endpoints? We need to know exact outbound endpoints to allow in permit lists.
[05:15] Lena: For hosted control plane, we'll provide a short allowlist for PrivateLink endpoints and our support IP ranges. For private control plane in your account, there should be no external outbound endpoints for inference traffic unless you configure them. For autoscaling or images, we can use your ECR and internal mirrors.
[05:30] Marta: How do you manage secrets — API keys or service credentials inside the runtime?
[05:33] Tom: Secrets are stored encrypted using the customer's KMS. We avoid static plaintext. For short-lived credentials we use IAM roles and assume-role patterns. We also support HashiCorp Vault integration if you run it.
[05:42] Carlos: SIEM integration — can we forward control plane logs as soon as they're generated? What's the format?
[05:46] Lena: Yes, logs can be forwarded in JSON lines to S3 or Kinesis; we provide a schema and example. We also support direct syslog/HTTP forwarding to SIEM via customer-managed endpoints.
[05:58] Priya: Any certifications beyond SOC2/ISO you can share? FedRAMP? HIPAA?
[06:02] Samir: Currently SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 artifacts available. We have HIPAA-compliant controls and BAAs available for healthcare customers, and some enterprise customers have done FedRAMP-equivalent assessments through private engagements. I'll share the artifacts.
[06:12] Carlos: For the pilot, we want to simulate denial of egress and ensure model loads still succeed. Can Redwood run entirely behind a proxy with no outbound internet?
[06:18] Lena: Yes if images are pre-pulled into your ECR and you run an internal mirror for OS packages. Some operational tasks (metrics, telemetry) can be configured to point to your internal endpoints. We'll need to define the scope for the pilot.
[06:28] Marta: When you talk about support access, are there break-glass procedures? We need an approval workflow and a time window.
[06:32] Tom: Yes, for hosted control plane we have a break-glass process: you raise a support ticket, approve the time window, and session actions are recorded. For private control plane you can keep Redwood out entirely and only grant access via a VPN or temporary user.
[06:42] Samir: Quick question from my side: Priya, what's your timeline and success criteria for this project?
[06:45] Priya: Timeline is end of Q3 for a production pilot, success criteria are: no PII leakage, <50ms p99 added latency for inference, audit trail visibility, and keys managed by us.
[06:54] Samir: Great that's actionable. We'll align the pilot to those success criteria.
[06:57] Carlos: Can we get an architecture diagram that shows ingress/egress, PrivateLink, and where keys live?
[07:00] Lena: Yes we'll send a diagram and a firewall rule set.
[07:03] Marta: Also a clear list of ports and IPs for allowlisting.
[07:06] Tom: We'll provide that plus a simple test plan for the pilot (what to exercise and metrics to capture).
[07:12] Priya: One more — data residency: if logs are forwarded to S3 in our account, who controls deletion and retention?
[07:16] Lena: You control lifecycle rules on that S3 bucket; we only push objects. You can set retention to 7 years as requested.
[07:22] Samir: We're about half an hour in. Any other technical blockers?
[07:26] Carlos: Just one: we need to map Redwood roles to our IdP groups and ensure admin privileges are limited.
[07:30] Tom: We support SCIM provisioning and group mapping. We'll show the default role sets and how to map them to your groups.
[07:36] Priya: Ok good.
[07:39] Samir: Quick detour — compliance questionnaire. We'll send a completed security questionnaire and also a SOC2 snapshot.
[07:46] Priya: Great. Also can we get a commitment that no model training data or customer prompts will be used to improve public models?
[07:52] Tom: For private deployments, data is not shared with public models. For hosted services we provide options to opt-out of data usage. We'll include contractual language in the next email.
[07:59] Carlos: For firewall logging, do you support VPC Flow Logs forwarding to our logging account?
[08:03] Lena: Yes, VPC Flow Logs can be sent to your logs account; we can surface network telemetry in the same SIEM pipeline.
[08:10] Marta: Any recommended hardening guides or runbooks?
[08:13] Samir: Yes, we'll include a deployment hardening checklist and runbook for incident response.
[08:18] Priya: Ok sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[08:21] Samir: Recap: Samir — send SOC2/ISO, security whitepaper; Lena — send VPC diagram, ports/IPs, pilot test plan; Tom — provide KMS/HSM options and support access flow; Customer — provide CIDR, egress constraints and timeline.
[08:35] Priya: That works. We'll review and get back with any additions.
[08:41] Carlos: Can we schedule the pilot kickoff next week?
[08:44] Samir: We'll propose a few times; I'll put a Doodle and propose next Wednesday/Thursday.
[08:49] Marta: Thanks everyone.
[08:50] Samir: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts after the call.
[08:53] Priya: Bye.
